rows.R: Confirmed: 9/64 - 6/62 = 4.385 pp, which rounds to 4.4, not the printed 4.3 (both cholesterol rows). Triglyceride (3.0) and glucose (-0.2) rows reproduce. Off by 0.1 pp in a post hoc table; interpretation unchanged. The printed CI (-8 to 17.2) also does not match Wald or Newcombe intervals and its method is not stated.
rows.evidence: jama_flint_2019_oi_190079.pdf PDF p.9 Table 5 (text extracted with PyMuPDF).
rows.rationale: Read Table 5: total and LDL rows both show 9 (14.1) vs 6 (9.7) with 4.3 (-8 to 17.2). Python: 9/64=0.140625, 6/62=0.096774, difference 4.385 pp -> 4.4 at one decimal; rounded percentages also give 4.4. Truncation would give 4.3. Other rows reproduce (4/64-2/62=3.02; 4/64-4/62=-0.20), so the error is specific to these rows. Additional check: Wald 95% CI = -6.9 to 15.6, Newcombe hybrid score = -7.4 to 16.1; neither reproduces -8 to 17.2, and only the other two rows are footnoted as exact CIs, so the CI method for these rows is unexplained (not part of the candidate as flagged). Error is real but 0.1 pp in a post hoc descriptive outcome; agree with AI domain.

rows.R: Confirmed: abstract and Secondary Outcomes give the HbA1c daily treatment-by-time estimate as -0.0002 mg/dL (95% CI -0.0021 to 0.0016), while Table 4 labels HbA1c in % and eFigure 8 uses HbA1c (%). mg/dL is not a valid HbA1c unit; the label looks carried over from the lipid estimates. The value itself is consistent with a % scale.
rows.evidence: jama_flint_2019_oi_190079.pdf PDF p.1 (abstract Results), p.7 (Secondary Outcomes), p.8 (Table 4, rendered image); joi190079supp2_prod.pdf PDF p.9 (eFigure 8).
rows.rationale: Verified the mg/dL label in both main-text locations, Table 4 row 'HbA1c, %' (baseline means 5.7-5.9) and the eFigure 8 axis 'HbA1c (%)' spanning 5.6-6.2. The coefficient magnitude (-0.0002 per day, about -0.05 over the 250-day trial) fits the % scale. The inconsistency is real, but HbA1c is never expressed in mg/dL, so readers can infer the intended unit and no numeric value changes. Kept the AI domain; graded minor_presentation rather than substantive.

rows.R: Confirmed within the protocol/data-analytic plan: section 4.2.1 says each of four sites will recruit 82 patients (=328), while Figure 1/3.9.1 (N=392), the text 'we plan to recruit 392 patients' and site Table 4 (98 per site; 98x4=392) agree on 392. No version, subset or phase label explains the 82, which appears in the human-subjects section, likely a leftover from an earlier draft. rows.R: Confirmed in the original MOP (Sept 2012) Table 1: enrollment through May 2015, 6-month follow-up through Dec 2015, but full 12-month follow-up 'through July 2015', earlier than both. May 2015 + 12 + 1 months is about June 2016; the April 2016 database lock is also earlier than that. Administrative projection only; no effect on trial conduct or results.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp2_prod.pdf PDF p.11 (MOP section 2.2, Table 1); searched the full 153-page supplement for any later timeline table (none found in the v4.5 final protocol).
rows.rationale: Read Table 1 directly. The 6-month row (Dec 2015) matches May 2015 + 6 months + 1-month window, so 'July 2015' for the 12-month follow-up endpoint is internally impossible; 'July 2016' would fit better but would then conflict with the April 2016 database-lock row. So the planning timeline is incoherent at more than one point. It is a real inconsistency within one planning document, but it is a projected administrative schedule in the original MOP, with no bearing on endpoints, populations or analyses. Kept AI domain plan_material; graded minor_presentation.

rows.R: The 12-month paragraph says 49 of 68 eligible failures switched, then gives 20/32 and 29/42, i.e., all 6-month failures (Table 2: 32+42=74). Excluding the 3+2 safety failures (eligibility criterion stated) gives 69, not 68. Mixed denominators and an unreconciled 68; numerators and arm percentages are correct. Descriptive, not an outcome estimate.
rows.evidence: jama_rathinam_2019_oi_190092.pdf PDF p.7 (Prespecified 12-Month Outcomes), p.6 (Table 2 failure counts and reasons), p.3 (Figure 1 flow).
rows.rationale: Python: 20+29=49; 32+42=74; 20/32=62.5%, 29/42=69.0%; 49/68=72.1% vs 49/74=66.2%. The text defines eligibility as failure without a serious laboratory adverse event; Table 2 lists safety failures 3/32 and 2/42 (defined as lab results meeting the SAE threshold), so 74-5=69, not 68. Figure 1 '3 not eligible due to safety' and '2 not eligible due to safety' give the same 69. The sentence therefore mixes an eligible denominator with all-failure arm denominators, and 68 cannot be reproduced. Probable rather than confirmed because one further ineligible patient for an unstated reason could explain 68. Minor: does not affect any comparative estimate.

rows.R: Exclude. Article: permuted blocks of 4 and 6. Only the Sept 2012 MOP says 4, 6 or 8; the original SAP (29 Jan 2013) and final SAP v1.5 (Mar 2017) both specify blocks of 4 (p=2/3) and 6 (p=1/3), matching the article; the final protocol v4.5 gives no sizes. The difference is a superseded early-draft detail with no bearing on validity.
rows.evidence: jama_rathinam_2019_oi_190092.pdf PDF p.2 (Randomization); joi190092supp2_prod.pdf PDF p.13 (MOP 2.4, Sept 2012) and v4.5 section 2.4 (no block sizes); joi190092supp3_prod.pdf PDF p.2 (SAP dated 29 Jan 2013), p.9 (2.4.3), p.42 and p.50 (v1.5 2.4.3).
rows.rationale: Verified all four sources. The governing randomization specification (SAP, both versions, the earliest predating enrollment) matches the report exactly; only the earliest MOP draft lists size 8, and the final protocol omits sizes. The apparent mismatch has a satisfactory documentary explanation, so exclude rather than retain as a protocol-report difference. AI suggested retain; I disagree.

rows.R: Confirmed. Final MOP v4.5 2.5.1 (referenced by the SAP as the success definition) requires no periocular/intravitreal corticosteroid injection after day 90. The article's 3-part success definition omits it and calls such injections protocol deviations; 4 MTX and 4 MMF patients had them. How these 8 were classified is not stated. Primary-endpoint definition difference.
rows.evidence: jama_rathinam_2019_oi_190092.pdf PDF p.3 (Outcomes definition; injections paragraph), p.6 (8 post-day-90 injections); joi190092supp2_prod.pdf PDF p.80 (image-only page, rendered and read: section 2.5.1); joi190092supp3_prod.pdf PDF p.70 (SAP 3.5.1 sensitivity analysis), SAP line defining success per MOP 2.5.1.
rows.rationale: Protocol p.80 is a scanned page; I rendered it and read 2.5.1 directly: success requires controlled inflammation, 7.5 mg/day prednisone, no injections after first 90 days, <=2 drops. The SAP defines success 'as defined in the Manual of Operations Section 2.5.1' and adds a sensitivity analysis classifying post-90-day injections by inflammation status at injection. The article lists only criteria (1)-(3) without the injection condition. Up to 8 patients (4 vs 4) could be classified differently, which is unlikely to change the OR materially but is a difference in the primary-outcome definition, so substantive_difference describes it. Kept AI domain.

rows.R: Missed doses 4.6% (SD 1.0) vs 4.3% (SD 0.5), Welch test, P=.87 cannot all be right: Welch P is .009 with n=96/98 and .006 with 107/108. 10 of 194 patients missed >=20% (sensitivity n=184), which needs an SD of at least about 3.5, so the 'SD' values cannot be SDs. If they are SEs, P is about .86-.87. The dispersion label (or P) is wrong; extracted SDs would be off about 10-fold.
rows.evidence: jama_rathinam_2019_oi_190092.pdf PDF p.4 (Statistical Analysis: Welch t test for missed doses), p.6 (Results text and Table 2 missed-dose row), p.7 (Figure 2 footnote e, n=184 for <20% missed).
rows.rationale: Python (scipy): Welch t=2.63, df=139.1, P=0.0094 for n=96/98; t=2.78, P=0.0061 for 107/108. Treating 1.0 and 0.5 as SEs: t=0.3/1.118=0.27 (P=0.79); with rounding limits (diff 0.20, SEs 1.05/0.55) t=0.169, P=0.866, i.e., compatible with .87. Independent check: the <20% sensitivity analysis kept 184 of 194, so 10 patients missed >=20%; with overall mean about 4.45 their contribution alone implies SD >= sqrt(10*15.55^2/193)=3.5, impossible with arm SDs of 1.0 and 0.5. So the printed mean (SD) and P are mutually incompatible, most likely because SEs are labelled SD. This differs from the AI rationale, which implies P is wrong; the P value is probably right and the SD label wrong. Either way the issue is confirmed and affects extractable values.

rows.R: Confirmed. Main Table 3 heads the MMF column n=109 (randomized), but all 30 MMF percentages reproduce with 108 (only 9 also reproduce with 109), and eTables 4-6 label MMF N=108. Footnote b says one MMF patient never received drug, so the intended treated denominator is inferable, but the header does not match the percentages.
rows.evidence: jama_rathinam_2019_oi_190092.pdf PDF p.8 (Table 3 and footnote b); joi190092supp1_prod.pdf PDF p.10-12 (eTables 4-6 headers N=108).
rows.rationale: Python: checked all 30 MMF count/percentage cells of Table 3; every one matches count/108 at one decimal, 9 coincidentally also match /109 (e.g., 19/108=17.6 vs 19/109=17.4; 59/108=54.6 vs 59/109=54.1). Supplement headers say N=108. The table therefore uses n=109 in the header and 108 as the denominator. The footnote explains why, so the meaning is recoverable and no estimate changes; minor presentation inconsistency. Kept AI domain.

rows.R: Confirmed. eTable 9 (switchers) MMF N=20, serious systemic diarrhea 1 (3.4); 1/20 = 5.0%. 3.4% is 1/29, the MTX column denominator, and other MMF count-1 cells in the same table show 5.0. Single-cell percentage error; the count is clear.

Confirmed but presentation-level in a supplementary safety table; the count of 1 event is unambiguous.

rows.R: Confirmed. eTable 1 defines ocular hypertension >=24 mm Hg as nonserious and 'surgery required' as serious. eTable 8 lists 'Ocular hypertension >24mm Hg' under both Non-Serious and Serious Ocular (serious row MTX 1, MMF 0); eTable 9 labels the serious row 'surgery required'. rows.evidence: joi190092supp1_prod.pdf PDF p.5 (eTable 1), p.14 (eTable 8), p.15 (eTable 9).

rows.R: Protocol (6 Jan 2019) Matching Process says each nonsurgical patient will be matched to five surgical patients, but its own sensitivity section specifies 1:5 matching on nonsurgical index dates. The article matches each surgical patient to 5 controls (2287 x 5 = 11,435). The protocol sentence is inverted wording; planned and reported design are the same.
rows.evidence: joi190103supp2_prod.pdf PDF p.2-3 (Study Protocol, Matching Process), p.6 (Sensitivity analyses: 1:1, 1:5, 1:10); jama_aminian_2019_oi_190103.pdf PDF p.1 (abstract), p.3-4 (Methods, Figure 1: 11 435 matched 1:5).
rows.rationale: Verified the protocol wording and the article counts; 2287 x 5 = 11,435. Only about 2,287 surgical patients were available against more than 39,000 nonsurgical patients, so matching five surgical patients to each control is infeasible, and the protocol's own 1:5 sensitivity language confirms the intended direction. The difference is a wording slip in the plan rather than a change in conduct, so minor_presentation rather than substantive_difference. Retained as a descriptive protocol-report record. Kept AI domain.

rows.R: Table 2 heart failure: 8-year KM incidence 18.9% (controls) - 6.8% (surgery) = 12.1 pp, but the ARD is printed as 12.9 (95% CI 10.4-15.1); the gap (0.8) exceeds rounding (possible 12.0-12.2). Composite and mortality rows reproduce exactly; all 5 component rows are larger by 0.3-0.9 and sit near their bootstrap-CI midpoints, which suggests a different estimand or population.
rows.evidence: jama_aminian_2019_oi_190103.pdf PDF p.7 (Table 2 and footnote a), p.4 (Methods: KM incidence, ARD, percentile bootstrap); joi190103supp1_prod.pdf PDF p.7 (eTable 5, same incidences).
rows.rationale: Python on Table 2: Primary 47.7-30.8=16.9 (printed 16.9), Secondary 10.6 (10.6), Mortality 7.8 (7.8), HF 12.1 vs 12.9, CAD 3.7 vs 4.2, Cerebrovascular 1.5 vs 1.8, Nephropathy 10.2 vs 11.1, AF 5.7 vs 6.5. Methods define the ARD as the difference in 8-year KM cumulative incidence, and footnote a uses the same definition. The 5 component-outcome rows (which use reduced at-risk subcohorts, e.g., HF 2049/10,093) all exceed the displayed difference, and the printed ARDs are close to the bootstrap CI midpoints (HF 12.75), so the ARD and CI may come from a different population or estimator than the displayed incidences. The displayed estimates contradict their stated definition, and the ARD is an extractable effect estimate (NNT changes), so I graded this confirmed and substantive.

rows.R: Table 2 coronary artery disease: 11.6% - 7.9% = 3.7 pp vs printed ARD 4.2 (1.9-6.8); the gap of 0.5 exceeds rounding (3.6-3.8 possible). This is part of a systematic pattern across all 5 component outcomes (printed ARD exceeds the displayed incidence difference), while composite and mortality rows reproduce. The extractable ARD is ambiguous (about 14% relative).
rows.evidence: jama_aminian_2019_oi_190103.pdf PDF p.7 (Table 2), p.4 (Methods); joi190103supp1_prod.pdf PDF p.7 (eTable 5).

The ARD contradicts its stated definition (difference in 8-year KM risk). The magnitude is modest in absolute terms but changes an extractable effect estimate (NNT about 27 vs 24), so substantive, direct.

Same systematic pattern as the other component outcomes. 1.5 vs 1.8 is a 20% relative difference in an extractable estimate whose CI touches zero.
rows.evidence: jama_aminian_2019_oi_190103.pdf PDF p.7 (Table 2), p.4 (Methods); joi190103supp1_prod.pdf PDF p.7 (eTable 5).

Given the CI is (-0.03, 3.4) and the HR P=.02, the point estimate matters for interpretation and extraction. Graded substantive for consistency with the other component rows.

rows.R: Table 2 nephropathy: 16.3% - 6.1% = 10.2 pp vs printed ARD 11.1 (8.8-13.6); the gap of 0.9 is far beyond rounding. It belongs to the systematic component-outcome pattern (printed ARDs near bootstrap-CI midpoints, not the KM incidence difference). The extractable ARD is ambiguous.

rows.R: Table 2 atrial fibrillation: 13.6% - 7.9% = 5.7 pp vs printed ARD 6.5 (4.4-8.7); the gap of 0.8 is beyond rounding (5.6-5.8 possible). Same systematic pattern across component outcomes. AF also violated proportional hazards per the text, so the 8-year ARD is the more interpretable summary, which makes the ambiguity matter more.

No displayed value or conclusion depends on it. AI suggested retain; I exclude.

rows.R: Confirmed impossible value: eTable 2 (MI, all randomized) intervention red wine baseline 33 (0, 29) g/week under a 'median (IQR)' footnote; a median cannot exceed Q3. rows.R: Confirmed. Baseline weight is 86.7 (13.0) / 86.4 (13.0) kg in Table 1 but 86.5 (12.9) / 86.3 (13.0) in eTable 9's all-randomized MI panel with the same Ns. eTable 9 is labelled multiple imputation and it is not stated whether baseline risk factors were imputed, which could explain the difference. rows.R: Confirmed. Baseline BMI is 32.5 (3.4/3.5) in Table 1 and 32.6 (3.4/3.5) in eTable 9's all-randomized MI panel (same Ns); eTable 9's completers panel shows 32.5. Weight moves the other way (C006), so a single rounding convention does not explain both. Undocumented baseline imputation may contribute. A 0.1 kg/m2 difference is immaterial.
rows.evidence: jama_saynorea main PDF p.4 (Table 1); joi190106supp3_prod PDF p.23 (eTable 9, MI and completers panels).
rows.rationale: Verified values. BMI is 0.1 higher in eTable 9 while weight is 0.1-0.2 lower, so the discrepancy is not a simple rounding shift; the cause cannot be determined. Real but trivial in magnitude. Minor presentation. Kept AI domain.

rows.R: Confirmed. Methods define clinically meaningful change as reductions of 'at least' 5% (weight, BMI, waist, lipids), at least 5 mm Hg SBP or 2.5 mm Hg DBP, and an HDL increase of at least 5%; Figure 4 panels say '>5%', '>10%', '>5 mm Hg', and 'Reduction 2.5 mm Hg' with no operator.
